hints: Recall that initial rate is the gradient of the curve at time zero, so think about where you would draw a tangent that just touches the curve at the start.
walkthrough:
Picture what initial rate means**
At the very start the concentrations are exactly known and no products have built up to interfere. So you need the steepness of the curve right at $t = 0$. Place a ruler so it just touches the curve at $(0, 0.80)$ and follows its direction, then extend it as a straight tangent line.

Turn the tangent into a number**
Pick two widely spaced points on your tangent line, not on the curve, read off $\Delta y = \Delta[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]$ and $\Delta x = \Delta t$, then calculate $$\text{initial rate} = -\frac{\Delta[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]}{\Delta t}$$ The negative sign is dropped because rate is reported as a positive decrease in reactant. A good tangent gives about $0.02$ to $0.03\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{ min}^{-1}$.
Final answer: Draw tangent to curve at $t = 0$ and calculate its gradient, $\text{rate} = -\Delta[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}] / \Delta t \approx 0.016$ to $0.040\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{ min}^{-1}$.

hints: Think about what happens to the concentration of a reactant present in very large excess as the limiting reactant is used up.
walkthrough:
Use the isolation idea**
The true rate equation is $\text{rate} = k[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}][\text{I}^{-}]$. If $[\text{I}^{-}]$ is huge compared to $[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]$, the small amount of $\text{I}^{-}$ used up makes almost no percentage change. So $[\text{I}^{-}]$ stays constant and can be absorbed into an observed constant $k' = k[\text{I}^{-}]$. The reaction then shows pseudo first order behaviour in $[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]$, which has a constant half-life.

Final answer: $[\text{I}^{-}]$ remains effectively constant during the reaction, so $\text{rate} = k[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}][\text{I}^{-}]$ behaves as first order in $[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]$ only and half-life can be used.

hints: Remember a homogeneous catalyst works by being used up in one step and regenerated in a later step through an alternative route.
Think of pairing $\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ as oxidant for $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in one step, and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ as oxidant for $\text{I}^{-}$ in the other step.
walkthrough:
See why the direct reaction is slow**
Reaction 1 brings together two negative ions, $\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$. Like charges repel, so collision is difficult and $E_a$ is high. $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is positive, so it is attracted to each anion in turn.

Build the two-step cycle**
First $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is oxidised by persulfate: $$2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ Then the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ formed oxidises iodide and regenerates the catalyst: $$2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{I}_2$$ Adding the two steps cancels $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ to give the overall reaction 1, proving catalytic behaviour.

hints: Recall whether the rate constant $k$ depends on concentration or only on temperature and activation energy.
walkthrough:
Link temperature to k and rate**
Higher temperature shifts the Boltzmann distribution so a larger fraction of molecules have energy at least $E_a$. Collisions are also more frequent. Therefore $k$ increases, and since $\text{rate} = k[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}][\text{I}^{-}]$, the rate at given concentrations also increases.
Final answer: Both the rate constant, $k$, and the rate of reaction 1 increase with increasing temperature.

hints: Identify the order with respect to the reactant that changes, then recall the half-life expression that applies only to first order reactions.
walkthrough:
Apply the first order half-life formula**
Reaction 2 is first order in $[\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}]$ and zero order in $[\text{H}^{+}]$, so overall it is first order with constant half-life. Use: $$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.693}{k}$$ Substitute $k = 1.58 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$: $$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{1.58 \times 10^{-2}} = 43.9\ \text{s}$$

hints: Remember the slow step must contain exactly the species that appear in the rate equation, with matching stoichiometric numbers.
Check that your two proposed steps add together to give the overall equation $2\text{NO} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NOBr}$, cancelling any intermediate.
walkthrough:
Let the orders design the slow step**
Rate is first order in $\text{NO}$ and first order in $\text{Br}_2$. The rate-determining step is the only step that controls rate, so it must involve one $\text{NO}$ molecule and one $\text{Br}_2$ molecule and nothing else. Write it as: $$\text{NO(g)} + \text{Br}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{NOBr}_2\text{(g)}$$ This creates the intermediate $\text{NOBr}_2$. An equivalent valid version produces $\text{NOBr} + \text{Br}$.

Complete the cycle to match the overall equation**
The second fast step must consume the intermediate and supply the remaining $\text{NO}$ to reach $2\text{NOBr}$ overall: $$\text{NOBr}_2\text{(g)} + \text{NO(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{NOBr(g)}$$ Adding step 1 and step 2 cancels $\text{NOBr}_2$ to give $2\text{NO} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NOBr}$. Because step 1 matches the orders, step 1 is the rate-determining step.

Final answer: step 1 (slow, rate-determining): $\text{NO} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{NOBr}_2$ (or $\text{NO} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{NOBr} + \text{Br}$)
step 2: $\text{NOBr}_2 + \text{NO} \rightarrow 2\text{NOBr}$ (or $\text{Br} + \text{NO} \rightarrow \text{NOBr}$)
rate-determining step = step 1
